stem: When is Boxing Day?
explanation: Boxing Day is the day after Christmas Day, 26 December. It is a public holiday.

stem: What is New Year's Eve called in Scotland?
explanation: In Scotland, 31 December is called Hogmanay. For some Scottish people it is a bigger celebration than Christmas.

stem: What do people remember on Bonfire Night, 5 November?

options.label: A failed plot to blow up Parliament in 1605
The end of the First World War

explanation: In 1605 a group of Catholics, including Guy Fawkes, tried to blow up the Houses of Parliament. People mark this with fireworks and bonfires.

stem: Why do many people wear poppies in early November?

options.label: To remember people who died in wars
To mark the start of winter

explanation: Remembrance Day is 11 November. People wear red poppies to remember those who died fighting for the UK and its allies.

stem: When is Valentine's Day?
explanation: On Valentine's Day, 14 February, people send cards or gifts to someone they love.

stem: On 1 April, people traditionally play jokes on each other until midday.
explanation: April Fool's Day is on 1 April. People play jokes on each other, but only until midday.

stem: Which TWO of these are Christian festivals?
explanation: Christmas celebrates the birth of Jesus and Easter remembers his death and resurrection. Diwali is a Hindu and Sikh festival and Hanukkah is Jewish.

stem: On which date is Halloween?
explanation: Halloween is on 31 October. Children often dress up and go 'trick or treating'.

stem: When is Mothering Sunday (Mother's Day) celebrated in the UK?
explanation: Mothering Sunday is held three weeks before Easter. It is a traditional day to honor mothers and often involves giving cards or flowers.

stem: On which day is St Patrick's Day celebrated?
explanation: St Patrick is the patron saint of Northern Ireland. His feast day is 17 March and it is a public holiday in Northern Ireland.

stem: Which religious festival marks the end of Ramadan, the month of fasting?
explanation: Eid al-Fitr is a Muslim festival that celebrates the end of fasting. People often enjoy special meals and give to charity during this time.

stem: What is often called the 'Festival of Lights' and is celebrated by Hindus and Sikhs?
explanation: Diwali is a major festival for Hindus and Sikhs. It celebrates the victory of light over darkness and good over evil.

stem: Which TWO of these statements about bank holidays are correct?

options.label: They fall on the same dates every year
Everyone in the UK must have the day off
There are several bank holidays every year

explanation: Bank holidays are public holidays when most banks and businesses close. They are held at different times, such as in the spring and late summer.

stem: What is a 'pantomime' in British tradition?

options.label: A comedy play based on a fairy tale

explanation: Pantomimes are funny plays traditionally performed at Christmas. They are often based on well-known fairy tales and involve audience participation.

stem: Roast turkey is a traditional food for Christmas dinner in the UK.
explanation: Many people in the UK eat roast turkey for their main Christmas meal. Other traditional items include Christmas pudding and mince pies.

stem: Which tradition was popularized in the UK by Queen Victoria's husband, Prince Albert?
explanation: Prince Albert brought the tradition of the Christmas tree to the UK from Germany. It became a common custom during the 19th century.

stem: Which religious group celebrates Vaisakhi to remember the founding of the Khalsa?
explanation: Vaisakhi is an important Sikh festival. It celebrates the founding of the Khalsa (the community of initiated Sikhs) by Guru Gobind Singh.

stem: Hanukkah is a Jewish festival that lasts for eight days.
explanation: Hanukkah is the Jewish Festival of Lights. It lasts for eight days and remembers the miracle of the oil in the Temple.

stem: What does the Christian festival of Good Friday commemorate?

options.label: The arrival of the Wise Men

explanation: Good Friday marks the day Jesus Christ died on the cross. It is followed by Easter Sunday, which celebrates his return to life.

stem: When is Father's Day celebrated in the UK?
explanation: Father's Day is a day to celebrate fathers and father figures. It is held on the third Sunday in June.

stem: Which TWO things are traditionally associated with Easter in the UK?
explanation: People often give chocolate eggs at Easter to represent new life. Hot cross buns, which are sweet breads with a cross on top, are also a traditional food.

stem: Lent is the period of 40 days before Easter when some people give up certain foods.
explanation: Lent is a time of reflection and fasting in the Christian calendar. It lasts for 40 days leading up to the celebration of Easter.

stem: In Scotland, what is the tradition of 'first footing' on New Year's Day?

options.label: Being the first guest to enter a home

explanation: First footing is a Scottish tradition where the first person to visit a home in the New Year brings gifts like coal to bring luck.

stem: When is St Andrew's Day, the national day of Scotland?
explanation: St Andrew's Day is celebrated on 30 November. It is Scotland's national day and is a bank holiday there.

stem: Which of these is the holiest day of the year in Judaism, marked by a 25-hour period of fasting?
explanation: Yom Kippur is the holiest day of the Jewish year. It is a day of fasting and prayer when Jewish people ask for forgiveness.

stem: Which religious festival is celebrated by Buddhists to remember the birth, enlightenment and death of the Buddha?
explanation: Wesak is an important festival for Buddhists. It takes place in May and is a time for people to visit temples and give gifts.

stem: What sweet, fruit-filled pies are traditionally eaten at Christmas in the UK?
explanation: Mince pies are small, sweet pastries filled with dried fruits and spices. They are a popular food during the Christmas season in the UK.

stem: On what date is Remembrance Day, which commemorates those who died in wars?
explanation: Remembrance Day is on 11 November. At 11:00 am, people observe a two-minute silence to remember those who died fighting for their country.

stem: Who makes a traditional television and radio broadcast to the nation on Christmas Day?
explanation: The Monarch (the King or Queen) makes a speech to the UK and the Commonwealth on Christmas Day. This tradition was started by King George V in 1932.

stem: What is the historical origin of the name 'Boxing Day'?

options.label: Giving small boxes of gifts or money to workers
A traditional sport played on the day after Christmas
Packing up Christmas decorations into cardboard boxes
The royal family collecting charity boxes from the public

explanation: Boxing Day, on 26 December, traditionally got its name from the practice of giving small boxes of money or food to servants and tradespeople.

stem: What is the British tradition of making a promise to behave better or stop a bad habit in the new year called?
explanation: A New Year's resolution is a promise that people make to improve their lives starting on 1 January. Common resolutions include eating healthier or exercising more.

stem: Northern Ireland has more bank holidays than England and Wales.
explanation: Northern Ireland has ten bank holidays a year, while England and Wales have eight. Scotland has nine bank holidays.

stem: Ash Wednesday marks the beginning of the Christian period known as Lent.
explanation: Ash Wednesday is the first day of Lent, which is a 40-day period of fasting and prayer before Easter.

stem: Which TWO of the following are Jewish festivals?
explanation: Rosh Hashanah (the Jewish New Year) and Yom Kippur (the Day of Atonement) are two major festivals in Judaism. Wesak is Buddhist and Diwali is Hindu.

stem: Which TWO of these dates are bank holidays in all parts of the UK?
explanation: Christmas Day and New Year's Day are official bank holidays in England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. National saint days are not bank holidays in all parts of the UK.
